title: Opioid Use Disorder: Offer Evidence-Based Agonist Treatment and Overdose Prevention
bottomLine: Opioid use disorder is a treatable chronic condition. Offer evidence-based opioid agonist treatment, overdose prevention and harm reduction rather than requiring detoxification or abstinence first; withdrawal management alone is not definitive OUD treatment and carries high relapse/overdose risk.
recognize: Loss of control, craving, tolerance/withdrawal and continued use despite harm support OUD; illicit supply exposure increases unpredictable fentanyl/toxic-drug risk.
Reduced tolerance after abstinence raises overdose risk.
differentiate: Physiologic dependence from prescribed opioids is not automatically OUD; diagnosis requires a problematic behavioural/clinical pattern.
Withdrawal is usually not life-threatening but can drive rapid return to use; overdose is a respiratory emergency.
assessment: Assess current/last opioid, route, overdose history, withdrawal, other sedatives/alcohol, pain, pregnancy, mental health/suicide, infections, housing and treatment goals.
workup: Use urine drug testing selectively to inform care rather than punish; check pregnancy/infection/liver/renal/ECG data when treatment choice or clinical presentation requires it.
management: Offer first-line opioid agonist treatment according to current CRISM guidance, naloxone/overdose education and harm-reduction supports; do not withhold care because abstinence is not the current goal.
Coordinate pain, mental-health, infectious-disease and social care.
medicationSafety: Induction/titration depends on agent, withdrawal state and fentanyl exposure; follow current Canadian protocols rather than an obsolete one-size-fits-all induction.
Benzodiazepines/alcohol increase respiratory risk but should prompt safety management, not automatic denial of OAT.
counselling: Use person-first non-stigmatizing language and provide naloxone education to patient/supports.
followUp: Use low-barrier frequent early follow-up and adjust treatment after recurrence rather than discharging the patient.
examTrap: Sending a patient to detox without offering OAT, then assuming relapse represents treatment failure rather than predictable overdose risk.
oneLinePearl: OUD treatment is agonist therapy plus harm reduction and continuity—not detox alone.
sourceBasis: CRISM National Guideline for Clinical Management of Opioid Use Disorder — 2024 update

title: Tobacco Cessation: Ask, Advise, Treat Nicotine Dependence, and Follow Up
bottomLine: Smoking cessation works best when behavioural support is paired with effective quit medication when appropriate. Ask routinely, assess nicotine dependence/readiness and past attempts, offer counselling plus NRT/varenicline/bupropion as clinically suitable, and treat lapse as a reason to adjust—not abandon—the plan.
recognize: Nicotine withdrawal includes craving, irritability, restlessness, sleep/concentration change and appetite change.
Health benefits of quitting occur at any age; repeated attempts are common.
differentiate: Commercial tobacco dependence should be discussed separately and respectfully from sacred/ceremonial tobacco use in Indigenous communities.
Vaping products are not the same as Health Canada-authorized cessation medications.
assessment: Ask tobacco/nicotine products, frequency/time-to-first use, prior attempts/medications, pregnancy, mental health, cardiovascular history, medications and patient goals.
workup: No laboratory testing is required to begin cessation treatment; targeted testing follows comorbidity, not nicotine dependence itself.
management: Provide brief behavioural counselling and quit support; use combination long-acting plus short-acting NRT or prescription pharmacotherapy when appropriate and preferred.
Link to provincial/territorial quit services and plan for triggers/lapse.
medicationSafety: Choose medication based on contraindications, pregnancy/reproductive context, mental-health history, interactions and prior response.
Do not imply nicotine replacement carries the same disease risk as continued combustible tobacco exposure.
redFlags: Acute psychiatric instability during quit attempt
Severe cardiovascular event requiring coordinated treatment rather than cessation delay
counselling: Use motivational, non-shaming language and separate tobacco dependence from cultural tobacco practices.
followUp: Follow soon after quit date/medication start and adjust for cravings, adverse effects and lapse.
examTrap: Telling a patient to quit without offering counselling or medication—or presenting vaping as an approved prescription cessation treatment in Canada.
oneLinePearl: Treat nicotine dependence like a chronic condition: medication plus support plus repeated follow-up.
sourceBasis: Health Canada Quit with Confidence resources

title: Insomnia: Diagnose the Sleep Problem Before Reaching for Sedation
bottomLine: Chronic insomnia is persistent difficulty initiating/maintaining sleep with daytime impact despite adequate opportunity. Evaluate schedule, OSA/restless legs/circadian disease, mood, substances, pain and medications; CBT-I is first-line and chronic sedative prescribing should not replace diagnosis.
recognize: Conditioned arousal, variable schedule and excess time awake in bed perpetuate insomnia.
Daytime sleepiness can signal OSA or medication effects rather than primary insomnia.
differentiate: Mania causes decreased need for sleep rather than distress about inability to sleep.
OSA, restless legs, circadian disorders and parasomnias have distinct histories and treatments.
assessment: Review sleep schedule, naps, caffeine/alcohol/cannabis, medications, snoring/apneas, leg symptoms, pain, mood/anxiety, work schedule and daytime safety.
workup: Sleep study is for suspected sleep-disordered breathing/other defined sleep disorders, not routine primary insomnia.
management: Use CBT-I including stimulus control/sleep consolidation and treat contributing disorders; use medication only selectively with clear indication/duration/reassessment.
medicationSafety: Benzodiazepines/Z-drugs cause dependence, falls/cognitive impairment and interaction with opioids/alcohol; sedating OTC anticholinergics are poor routine choices.
counselling: Explain how behavioural sleep treatment retrains sleep drive rather than merely sedating wakefulness.
followUp: Track sleep efficiency/daytime function and taper chronic sedatives when appropriate.
examTrap: Starting nightly benzodiazepines before asking about OSA, bipolar symptoms, alcohol and daytime impairment.
oneLinePearl: Insomnia treatment changes sleep behaviour; sedation alone does not fix the disorder.
sourceBasis: Choosing Wisely Canada Geriatrics/Hospital Pharmacy sleep recommendations

title: Eating Disorders: Medical Instability Can Occur at Any Body Size
bottomLine: Eating-disorder severity is determined by behaviour, physiologic instability and psychiatric risk—not appearance or BMI. Ask about restriction, bingeing, purging and compulsive exercise, assess orthostasis/electrolytes/ECG and suicide risk when indicated, and urgently refer medically unstable patients.
recognize: Restriction, bingeing, vomiting/laxatives/diuretics, compulsive exercise and intense weight/shape concern occur across anorexia, bulimia, binge-eating and other disorders.
Atypical anorexia can cause severe malnutrition despite normal/high BMI.
differentiate: ARFID is driven by sensory/aversive/low-interest factors rather than weight/shape concerns.
GI/endocrine disease, depression and diabetes can change weight/appetite but do not by themselves establish an eating disorder.
assessment: Ask privately about intake, binge/purge methods, exercise, weight trajectory, syncope/chest symptoms, menses/endocrine effects, substances and suicide/self-harm; check orthostatic vitals/temperature and hydration.
workup: Use electrolytes, glucose, magnesium/phosphate, CBC, renal/liver tests and ECG according to restriction/purging/instability; testing does not replace clinical severity assessment.
management: Urgently manage medical instability; use evidence-based multidisciplinary psychotherapy/nutrition/medical monitoring and specialty eating-disorder care.
medicationSafety: Bupropion is contraindicated in anorexia/bulimia because of seizure risk; QT-prolonging drugs are hazardous with electrolyte disturbance.
Refeeding high-risk malnutrition requires electrolyte/clinical monitoring.
counselling: Use weight-neutral, non-shaming language and focus on medical recovery/function.
followUp: Track vitals, behaviours, labs when indicated, weight trajectory and psychiatric safety with the treatment team.
examTrap: Reassuring a normal-BMI patient who has rapid loss, bradycardia and daily purging.
oneLinePearl: Eating-disorder severity is physiology and behaviour—not visible body size.

title: Adult ADHD: Prove the Developmental Pattern and Treat Functional Impairment
bottomLine: Adult ADHD is a neurodevelopmental condition with symptoms beginning in childhood and persistent impairment across settings. Current concentration problems alone—especially during depression, anxiety, sleep loss or substance use—do not establish ADHD; rating scales support but do not replace developmental assessment.
recognize: Chronic disorganization, distractibility, impulsivity and task-completion difficulty can persist into adult education/work/relationships.
differentiate: Depression/anxiety/PTSD/sleep deprivation/substances and bipolar disorder can mimic or coexist; mania is episodic with abnormal mood/energy/decreased need for sleep.
assessment: Establish childhood onset/developmental history, impairment in multiple settings, collateral where available, sleep, mood/anxiety, trauma, substance use, learning history and cardiovascular history.
workup: No routine neuroimaging/lab test diagnoses ADHD; use targeted testing for mimics and validated rating tools as adjuncts.
management: Use environmental/organizational/psychological supports plus evidence-based stimulant or nonstimulant pharmacotherapy based on impairment, preference and risk.
medicationSafety: Monitor BP/HR, appetite/weight, sleep, mood, misuse/diversion and interactions; routine ECG is not required for every patient without cardiac risk/history.
counselling: Set functional goals and discuss safe storage/diversion prevention.
followUp: Track function and adverse effects, not only symptom scores.
examTrap: Diagnosing adult ADHD solely from current concentration problems during untreated depression with no childhood history.
oneLinePearl: Adult ADHD is a lifelong pattern—not a new adult attention symptom.

title: PTSD: Trauma-Informed Diagnosis and Evidence-Based Recovery Without Forced Disclosure
bottomLine: PTSD requires a trauma-related pattern of intrusion, avoidance, negative mood/cognition and hyperarousal with impairment after the appropriate duration. Trauma-informed care prioritizes safety, choice and control; the clinician does not need to force a detailed trauma narrative before validating symptoms or starting evidence-based treatment.
recognize: Nightmares, flashbacks, avoidance, hypervigilance, guilt/numbing and physiologic reactivity are common; somatic symptoms and high health-care use can occur.
differentiate: Acute stress reactions, depression, panic, OCD, substance use and traumatic brain injury can overlap.
Psychosis/dissociation require careful phenomenology rather than assuming all unusual experiences are PTSD.
assessment: Ask permission before trauma questions; assess current safety, suicide/self-harm, dissociation, sleep, substances, ongoing violence and functional impairment.
workup: Use validated PTSD screens/severity tools as adjuncts; order medical/neurologic testing only when a plausible alternate diagnosis exists.
management: Use trauma-focused psychotherapy as core treatment and evidence-based pharmacotherapy for PTSD/comorbid symptoms when indicated; address ongoing safety and social needs.
medicationSafety: Avoid routine long-term benzodiazepines for PTSD; monitor medication-specific adverse effects/interactions and substance self-medication.
counselling: Explain that the patient controls the depth/timing of disclosure and treatment does not require recounting every detail at the first visit.
followUp: Track function, sleep, avoidance and safety and coordinate psychotherapy/specialty care.
examTrap: Insisting on a detailed trauma retelling in the first visit before offering care.
oneLinePearl: Trauma-informed care restores control; it does not demand a story as proof.

title: Personality Disorders: Recognize Enduring Patterns Without Using the Label as a Dismissal
bottomLine: Personality disorders are enduring inflexible patterns across contexts that cause distress/impairment and are diagnosed longitudinally—not from one difficult encounter. The label never replaces assessment of suicide risk, trauma, mood, psychosis, substance use or medical illness.
recognize: Borderline patterns can include affective instability, abandonment sensitivity, self-harm and unstable relationships; other personality patterns have different cognitive/interpersonal features.
differentiate: Bipolar disorder is episodic; PTSD/ADHD/autism/substance use can overlap with personality features.
Acute suicidality or psychosis is not 'just personality' and needs its own assessment.
assessment: Review longstanding patterns across relationships/work, developmental/trauma history, mood episodes, self-harm/suicide, substance use, psychosis, function and prior treatments.
workup: No laboratory test diagnoses personality disorder; targeted testing follows plausible medical/substance mimics.
management: Use structured evidence-based psychotherapy and consistent collaborative boundaries; treat comorbid mood/anxiety/substance conditions and crisis risk rather than prescribing to a personality label.
medicationSafety: Avoid polypharmacy aimed at rapidly controlling every affective/interpersonal symptom; prescribe only for defined target conditions with monitoring.
counselling: Use non-stigmatizing language and emphasize treatability, function and skills rather than character judgments.
followUp: Maintain continuity/clear care plans and reassess risk during crises/relationship transitions.
examTrap: Dismissing new suicidality as 'attention seeking' because a patient carries a borderline-personality diagnosis.
oneLinePearl: A personality diagnosis explains a pattern; it never excuses skipping a fresh safety assessment.

title: Suicide Risk: Ask Directly, Assess Dynamic Risk, Build a Specific Safety Plan
bottomLine: Suicide assessment is not prediction and no score can certify discharge safety. Ask directly about thoughts, intent, plan, access to means, recent behaviour, prior attempts, intoxication/psychosis and dynamic stressors, then choose a level of care capable of maintaining safety and create a collaborative safety plan when outpatient care is appropriate.
recognize: Recent attempt, current intent/plan/means, agitation, psychosis, intoxication, severe insomnia, hopelessness and transition/discharge periods increase acute concern.
differentiate: Passive death wish differs from active intent but still requires assessment.
Protective factors reduce risk but do not cancel specific active intent/means.
assessment: Ask ideation, intent, plan, rehearsal/preparation, means access, past attempts, self-harm, substances, psychosis, supports, dependents and ability/willingness to use a safety plan.
workup: Medical/toxicology assessment is indicated for overdose/intoxication/injury/delirium; screening scores do not replace interview/collateral/clinical judgment.
management: Imminent risk or inability to maintain safety requires emergency psychiatric/medical assessment and a secure setting.
Appropriate outpatient care includes a specific written safety plan, lethal-means reduction, treatment of underlying illness and rapid proactive follow-up.
medicationSafety: Consider overdose toxicity/dispensed quantities and sedative combinations while still treating the underlying disorder.
redFlags: Current intent with accessible lethal means
No viable safety support when required
counselling: Explain that asking directly about suicide does not create suicidal thoughts and involve trusted supports with consent when safe/appropriate.
followUp: Arrange rapid follow-up after crisis/discharge and document assessment, safety plan and ownership.
examTrap: Using a signed no-suicide contract or low screening score as the reason to discharge a patient with a specific plan and accessible means.
oneLinePearl: Risk assessment asks what may happen; safety planning specifies what happens instead.
sourceBasis: CAMH Assessment and Management of Suicide Risk

title: Psychopharmacology Basics: Diagnosis, Target Symptom, Time Course, Interactions, and Monitoring
bottomLine: Psychiatric prescribing starts with a defensible diagnosis/target, baseline risks and a monitoring plan. Know expected time course, common/serious adverse effects, withdrawal/rebound, interactions and what outcome defines success; avoid adding medications to treat side effects from an unreviewed regimen.
recognize: Antidepressants, antipsychotics, mood stabilizers, stimulants and sedatives have different onset/monitoring and toxicity profiles.
Treatment response includes function and tolerability, not symptom score alone.
differentiate: Medication nonresponse can reflect wrong diagnosis, inadequate dose/duration, nonadherence, interaction or untreated substance/medical disorder.
Side effects can mimic new psychiatric symptoms and create prescribing cascades.
assessment: Review diagnosis/target, prior response, bipolarity/suicide risk, substances, pregnancy, metabolic/cardiac/renal/hepatic risks, current medications and patient priorities.
workup: Order baseline/follow-up labs/ECG/levels only when required by the drug or patient risk; do not use routine broad panels for every psychotropic.
management: Choose evidence-based monotherapy where possible, titrate deliberately, define response timeline and only augment/polypharmacy when rationale/monitoring are explicit.
medicationSafety: Monitor serotonin toxicity, metabolic/movement/QT effects, lithium/valproate organ toxicity, stimulant CV/misuse risk and sedative dependence according to agent.
Avoid abrupt discontinuation when withdrawal/rebound is plausible.
counselling: Explain target benefit, expected onset, common harms and what symptoms require urgent contact.
followUp: Measure benefit/harm and reconcile the regimen at every meaningful change.
examTrap: Adding a second psychiatric drug to treat an adverse effect without reviewing whether the first drug is still indicated.
oneLinePearl: Every psychotropic needs a target, monitoring plan and exit strategy.
